video_title: WHOOP CEO, Will Ahmed: 50B Hours of Health Data, a 4 Million Member Data Moat, & the FDA Fight
gist: Jason Calacanis interviews Whoop CEO Will Ahmed: Whoop's growth accelerated from 1M members in 12 years to ~4M expected by year-end, wearers average 23.6 hrs/day for 50B+ hours of data, and the subscription model incentivizes software upgrades over annual hardware. Covers in-house foundation models inferring biomarkers, the FDA warning letter over blood pressure that ended with updated guidance, athlete strategy (LeBron as ambassador), and closing asides on SPVs and the 'anti-AI trade'.

insights.claim: Whoop took about 12 years to reach 1 million members, then about 18 months to 2 million, about 6 months to 3 million, and expects to end the year around 4 million members.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Member growth is sharply accelerating, a sign of compounding adoption in screenless wearables.
insights.quote: it took about 12 years for us to get to a million members and then another 18 months or so to 2 million, about 6 months to 3 million

insights.claim: Whoop membership costs roughly $15 to $30 per month depending on plan, and Whoop now has about 1,200 employees.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Gives the base for revenue-run-rate math on a subscription wearable.
insights.quote: Depending on what plan you're on, it's anywhere from 15 to $30 a month.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis floated hypothetical math of a $10 billion valuation, 4 million members and about $250 per member per year, implying roughly $1 billion in revenue; Ahmed did not confirm these figures.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Treat ~$1B revenue/$10B valuation as host speculation, not company disclosure.
insights.quote: let's say we're at a $10 billion valuation here. We got 4 million members, 250 on average a year

insights.claim: On average a Whoop member wears the device 23.6 hours a day, giving Whoop just over 50 billion hours of continuous physiological data, which Ahmed calls one of the largest health data sets in the world.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Wear-time is the core of the data moat that AI models train on.
insights.quote: On average, a Whoop member wears Whoop 23.6 hours a day.

insights.claim: Whoop's 2017 consumer launch at a one-time $500 fee showed strong retention but weak sales, prompting a switch to a subscription with a lower entry price that drove growth in 2018-19 and made Whoop a recurring-revenue business.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Converting high-engagement hardware into subscriptions solves the sales problem and earns a better investor multiple.
insights.quote: we quickly became a recurring revenue business versus a hardware business, which of course is more attractive to investors

insights.claim: Ahmed argues pure hardware companies are incentivized to ship new hardware every 12 months whether or not it is innovative, while Whoop's subscription model incentivizes step-function hardware launches and continuous software upgrades like ECG/AFib detection, advanced labs, healthspan and blood pressure insights on existing devices.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Subscription wearables compete on feature velocity on installed hardware, a different playbook from Apple's upgrade cycle.
insights.quote: when you're a hardware business, you're incentivized to ship new hardware every 12 months, whether or not it's actually innovative

insights.claim: Ahmed says being a subscription business changed Whoop's DNA by making it obsessed with existing members, engagement and behavior change rather than new-unit sales.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Retention-driven culture is a durable advantage for subscription consumer hardware.

insights.claim: Ahmed notes there were more competitive wearable products 10 years ago than today, citing the Jawbone/Fitbit era and Nike, Adidas and Under Armour exiting, while calling the Apple Watch the most successful smartwatch in the world.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: The screenless-wearable category has consolidated, with Apple the main potential threat.
insights.quote: 10 years ago, there were more competitive products in the market than there are today

insights.claim: Whoop says it does not sell member data and positions the membership, not the user, as the product, contrasting with ad-funded big tech and Apple's expensive-hardware model.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Privacy positioning supports willingness to share medical records and labs, feeding the data moat.
insights.quote: we do not sell data. You know, you are not the product, Jason.

insights.claim: Whoop is building its own foundation models trained on its physiological data combined with uploaded blood tests, advanced labs and medical records, and sees early signs it can predict an out-of-range biomarker like cortisol without measuring it directly.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Passive-sensor biomarker inference could enable targeted testing and a diagnostics layer on top of wearables.
insights.quote: we might be able to predict that a biomarker is out of range without actually measuring the biomarker itself

insights.claim: Just over 50% of Whoop members journal every day, members open the app about eight times a day, and about 80% of the member base interacts with the AI coach, which Ahmed says few companies can match.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Self-reported behavioral labels plus sensor data form a hard-to-replicate training set.
insights.quote: 80% of their member base interacting with the AI

insights.claim: Calacanis rated Whoop's AI coach, launched less than six months earlier, at about 7.5 out of 10, and Whoop spun up a dedicated team for travel and time-zone coaching because it is a popular use case.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: AI coaching is early but driving engagement; vertical use cases like travel are being productized.

insights.claim: Across Whoop's population, eating within 3 hours of bedtime is very detrimental to sleep and recovery; alcohol shows a hugely negative effect, with Ahmed's own alcohol impact at -9% on recovery.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Population-scale behavioral correlations are a product feature and potential research asset.
insights.quote: eating within 3 hours of bedtime, we've now seen across the entire Whoop population is really detrimental to your sleep and your recovery

insights.claim: HRV typically declines with age, from roughly 80-100 in your 20s to about 70 in your 30s, 50 in your 40s and 30s and below in your 50s-60s, so keeping HRV flat over years signals good fitness and longevity.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Long-run HRV baselines are a longevity metric that justifies continuous wear.

insights.claim: Ahmed cites member cases where wearable signals preceded diagnoses: abnormally high sleeping heart rate preceded stage four Hodgkin's lymphoma, and an HRV drop from about 100 to 50 preceded testicular cancer; Calacanis says Whoop flagged his COVID early enough to get Paxlovid.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed / Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Anecdotal early-warning value supports a shift from wellness toward preventive medicine, though not clinically validated.

insights.claim: Ahmed says about 50% of weight lost on GLP-1s is typically fat and 50% muscle, so Whoop's new GLP-1 tracker pushes users toward strength training, protein and step targets to avoid frailty.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: GLP-1 adoption creates adjacent demand for muscle-preservation coaching and monitoring.
insights.quote: typically speaking about 50% of the weight that someone loses is fat and 50% is muscle

insights.claim: Whoop recruited 70,000 members into a stress, sleep and blood pressure study, uploading cuff readings daily for weeks, to train a cuffless wrist blood pressure algorithm.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Member-sourced studies let consumer health firms generate clinical-scale data fast and cheaply.

insights.claim: The FDA sent Whoop a warning letter over its Blood Pressure Insights feature, but Ahmed says the FDA has since updated its guidelines, based partly on Whoop's case and industry feedback, to recognize wellness uses of blood pressure, and the feature remains available.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Regulatory line between wellness and medical devices is shifting in favor of consumer wearables.
insights.quote: the FDA actually has since updated their guidelines

insights.claim: Whoop runs a dual path with the FDA: its wrist ECG is an FDA-cleared 510(k) product, while other features are launched faster as wellness applications.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: A wellness-first, clearance-where-needed strategy speeds time to market for health features.

insights.claim: Whoop chose to partner with cuff makers like Omron for blood pressure calibration because cuffs are a commoditized technology, with the goal of eventually replacing the cuff, while usually defaulting to build or acquire over partnering.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Whoop targets replacing commoditized medical peripherals rather than making them.

insights.claim: Ahmed advises that pre-marketing-stage companies avoid paying anyone to use their product because a 24/7 wearable must be loved authentically; LeBron James wore Whoop for 11 years with no formal deal before becoming a global ambassador.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: Organic adoption by elite athletes is validating; paid endorsements only come once NIL has marketing value.
insights.quote: you should be really careful paying anyone to use your product

insights.claim: Australian Open players were asked to remove Whoops even though the ITF had approved them for matches, after which other tennis majors said wearables can be worn; the NBA is still reviewing in-game use.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed
insights.so_what: In-competition wearable approvals are expanding, opening data and branding opportunities.

insights.claim: Calacanis says his syndicate of 4,000 members launched a late-stage practice this year, doing deals in Zipline and Icon Homes, and advises getting the company CFO's blessing for SPV and secondary transactions.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Retail-accessible late-stage SPVs are proliferating, raising governance friction with issuers.

insights.claim: Ahmed and Calacanis warn that secondary brokers often claim to have shares at a price but are just fishing to create a market.
insights.speaker: Will Ahmed / Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Treat unverified private-share offers skeptically.

insights.claim: Calacanis says Uber is trading at an all-time-low P/E and lumps DoorDash, Uber and Figma into an 'anti-AI trade' that has been taken to the woodshed.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Possible value in AI-disruption-fear names, per a host aside.
insights.quote: the anti-AI trade, DoorDash, Uber, Figma
